title: Prioritization & Roadmap
definition: Domain leads who have a mandate and a rough idea but no clear path to their first workflow. This chapter walks from 'too many ideas' to a single, scoped, approved bet — and then from that bet through a 90-day roadmap that the build team can execute.

narrativeSections.heading: The context
narrativeSections.content: Before you can prioritize, you need two things that come out of the Engage phase: the tech & data readiness picture (which tells you where things can be built) and the business process map (which tells you where value should be built). Prioritization without both is either politically driven or technically naive — and usually both.

narrativeSections.heading: What you're doing
narrativeSections.content: Turn the outputs of Engage into a scored, comparable list of workflow candidates using a consistent prioritization framework. Apply objective criteria: value potential (cost base, impact on outputs), feasibility (data readiness, integration complexity, technical risk), and strategic fit (leadership priority, external benchmarks). Also surface things like unrealistic timelines and scope expectations early — this is when you correct them, not after the build has started.

narrativeSections.heading: The pain point
narrativeSections.content: Prioritization fails in predictable ways: teams gather impressions instead of data, then present recommendations that look like opinions to leaders who override them. Or they take on 'band-aid' projects that fix symptoms without addressing root causes. Or they scope something that couldn't realistically ship in 90 days and then miss the date.

narrativeSections.heading: Artifacts
narrativeSections.content: Prioritization Framework (with scoring rubric and benchmark comparison), completed for each candidate workflow.

artifacts.description: Scoring rubric and benchmark comparison, completed for each candidate workflow.

narrativeSections.heading: Overview
narrativeSections.content: You've chosen a candidate. Now you go deep on it before designing anything. This is the step where you find out whether the opportunity is real or imagined — and whether the data, systems, and user behavior actually support the hypothesis you used to prioritize it.

narrativeSections.heading: Gather
narrativeSections.content: Spend profile, skills inventory, KPI baseline, as-is process map, root causes of failure, external benchmarks from peer organizations. Talk directly to the people who do the work. The outside-in view (what does best-in-class look like?) prevents you from optimizing a broken process.

narrativeSections.heading: The pain point
narrativeSections.content: The go/no-go decision is hard because everyone fears failure and no one wants to call a stop. Make it easier: be explicit with your SteerCo from day one that Workflow Analysis is a time-boxed exercise whose purpose is to validate or invalidate the opportunity. Book the go/no-go meeting before the analysis starts. Arrive at it with a clear recommendation and the evidence to back it up.

narrativeSections.heading: Artifacts
narrativeSections.content: Workflow Analysis report (spend, skills, KPIs, as-is map, root causes, benchmarks). Workflow Analysis Outcome with go/no-go recommendation and reasoning.

artifacts.title: Workflow Analysis Report
artifacts.description: Spend, skills, KPIs, as-is map, root causes, benchmarks.

narrativeSections.heading: If no-go
narrativeSections.content: Document why, move to the next prioritized process. This is success, not failure.

narrativeSections.heading: Overview
narrativeSections.content: With a validated opportunity and executive approval, define the north-star vision and scope the MVP. The north star is what the fully transformed workflow looks like — unconstrained, blank slate. The MVP is the smallest thing you can build in 90 days that meaningfully tests the core hypothesis.

narrativeSections.heading: The pain point
narrativeSections.content: Poorly defined north star or requirements at this stage guarantee project failure downstream. Vague requirements produce vague software. The solution design output has to be specific enough that a developer can start without a clarification call. If it isn't, you're not done.

narrativeSections.heading: Artifacts
narrativeSections.content: High-Level Requirements Document (north star vision, MVP scope definition with explicit in/out list, build-vs-buy recommendation, target KPIs).

artifacts.title: High-Level Requirements Document
artifacts.description: North star vision, MVP scope definition with explicit in/out list, build-vs-buy recommendation, target KPIs.

sections.phaseTitle: Build with discipline, decide with data

narrativeSections.heading: 90-day build
narrativeSections.content: The team inherits the north star and requirements from Solution Design. Their first job — before writing a line of code — is to confirm they can deliver something to real users in 90 days that sufficiently tests the experimental hypothesis. They may need to spend time with the original designers to fully understand intent.

narrativeSections.heading: The 90-day roadmap
narrativeSections.content: The 90-day roadmap is built from this scoping: bucket requirements into prioritized releases, confirm what the go/no-go operational metrics are, and get building. User engagement and feedback is not optional — plan for it from the start.

narrativeSections.heading: De-scope decisions
narrativeSections.content: De-scope decisions will happen. That's the mechanism that makes 90-day delivery possible, not a sign of failure. A well-communicated de-scope with a post-MVP backlog keeps executive confidence intact.

narrativeSections.heading: Go/no-go decision
narrativeSections.content: At the end of 90 days, the data either supports scaling or it doesn't. The decision should be made on the metrics defined before the build started, not on enthusiasm or organizational momentum. Document the reasoning either way.

narrativeSections.heading: Post go/no-go — change management goes into high gear
narrativeSections.content: Change management should have started earlier (impact assessment, comms planning, UAT users identified). After go/no-go, the plan accelerates: training, rollout, old-process retirement, adoption monitoring with continuous KPI assessment.

narrativeSections.heading: Artifacts
narrativeSections.content: 90-day sprint roadmap, prioritized release plan, go/no-go recommendation with supporting metrics, post-MVP backlog, change management and adoption plan.

artifacts.description: Prioritized release plan with sprint cycles and deliverables.

designPrinciples.title: Inputs first
designPrinciples.description: The chapter opens not with 'how to prioritize' but with 'here's what Engage produced, and here's how to use it.' Grounds the reader before giving them a framework.

designPrinciples.title: Book the go/no-go before you start
designPrinciples.description: This is the single most actionable piece of advice and should be prominent, not buried.

designPrinciples.title: The build team re-validates scope
designPrinciples.description: The 90-day roadmap isn't just 'execute the design.' The build team has a responsibility to confirm the scope is achievable and flag it if it isn't.
